lessons.title: Introduction to Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the fundamental concept of numbers, their purpose in counting and measurement, and the structure of the real number system. Students learn why numbers are essential in mathematics and daily life.

blocks.text: 1.1 Introduction to Numbers

Numbers are the foundation of all mathematics. They allow us to count objects, measure quantities, and describe relationships. The real number system includes natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, irrational numbers, and real numbers. This lesson establishes the importance of numbers and previews how they are classified and used in various mathematical operations. Understanding the nature of numbers is essential for success in JAMB Mathematics, as every other topic depends on numerical reasoning.

lessons.title: Classification of Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson explores the hierarchy of number sets, including natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, irrational numbers, and real numbers, with clear definitions and examples.

blocks.text: 1.2 Classification of Numbers

Numbers are organized into sets based on properties. Natural numbers (1,2,3,...) are used for counting. Whole numbers add zero. Integers include negative numbers. Rational numbers can be written as p/q (q≠0) and have terminating or repeating decimals. Irrational numbers, such as √2 and π, have non-terminating, non-repeating decimals. Real numbers include all rational and irrational numbers. Understanding these classifications helps in identifying number types and applying appropriate rules in calculations.

lessons.title: Natural and Whole Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson focuses on natural numbers (counting numbers) and whole numbers (natural numbers plus zero), their properties, and their use in basic arithmetic.

blocks.text: 1.3 Natural and Whole Numbers

Natural numbers are positive integers (1,2,3,...) while whole numbers include zero (0,1,2,3,...). Both sets are closed under addition and multiplication, but not under subtraction or division. Natural numbers are the foundation of counting and ordering, and they appear in virtually every area of mathematics. Whole numbers extend the concept to include zero, which is essential for place value and algebra. This lesson also covers the number line and basic properties.

lessons.title: Integers
lessons.summary: This lesson covers positive and negative whole numbers and zero, including operations with integers, absolute value, and the integer number line.

blocks.text: 1.4 Integers

Integers include all positive and negative whole numbers and zero: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... They are used to represent quantities with direction (e.g., temperature, elevation). This lesson teaches addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of integers, with special attention to sign rules. The absolute value of an integer is its distance from zero on the number line. Understanding integers is crucial for algebra, coordinate geometry, and many word problems.

lessons.title: Rational Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson defines rational numbers as numbers expressible as p/q (q≠0), including terminating and recurring decimals, and explores operations with rational numbers.

blocks.text: 1.5 Rational Numbers

A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction p/q where p and q are integers and q≠0. Examples include ½, 0.75, and 0.333... (recurring). All integers are rational numbers because they can be expressed with denominator 1. This lesson covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rational numbers, as well as conversion between fractions, decimals, and percentages. Rational numbers are essential for financial mathematics, probability, and measurement.

lessons.title: Irrational Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson explains irrational numbers as numbers that cannot be expressed as a fraction, with examples such as √2, √3, and π.

blocks.text: 1.6 Irrational Numbers

Irrational numbers cannot be expressed as p/q. Their decimal expansions are non-terminating and non-repeating. Common examples include the square root of non-perfect squares (e.g., √2, √3) and mathematical constants like π (pi) and e. Surds are a special type of irrational number that involve roots. This lesson distinguishes rational from irrational numbers and introduces the concept of surds, which are treated extensively in later lessons.

lessons.title: Real Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson combines rational and irrational numbers into the set of real numbers, covering the real number line and the density property.

blocks.text: 1.7 Real Numbers

The set of real numbers is the union of all rational and irrational numbers. Every point on the number line corresponds to a real number. The real number system is ordered, meaning we can compare any two real numbers. It also satisfies the density property: between any two distinct real numbers, there exists another real number. This lesson also introduces the concept of intervals on the real number line, which is useful in solving inequalities and representing solutions.

lessons.title: The Number Line and Ordering of Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches how to represent numbers on a number line, compare values, and understand absolute value and ordering.

blocks.text: 1.8 The Number Line and Ordering of Numbers

The number line is a visual tool that represents numbers as points on a straight line. Numbers increase from left to right. This lesson teaches how to plot numbers, compare them using inequality symbols (<, >, ≤, ≥), and find the absolute value (distance from zero). Understanding the number line is essential for working with integers, fractions, and decimals, and for solving inequalities. It also helps in visualizing operations and properties of numbers.

lessons.title: Factors and Multiples
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces factors and multiples of numbers, including finding factor pairs and understanding multiples.

blocks.text: 1.9 Factors and Multiples

A factor of a number divides it exactly without leaving a remainder. A multiple is obtained by multiplying the number by an integer. This lesson covers finding all factors of a given number, listing multiples, and understanding the relationship between factors and multiples. These concepts are foundational for prime factorization, HCF, LCM, and simplifying fractions. The lesson also introduces the concept of common factors and common multiples, which are used in many JAMB problems.

lessons.title: Prime Numbers
lessons.summary: This lesson defines prime numbers (numbers with exactly two factors: 1 and itself) and teaches methods to identify primes.

blocks.text: 1.10 Prime Numbers

A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has exactly two distinct positive factors: 1 and itself. Examples are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13. Prime numbers are the building blocks of all integers, as every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes (prime factorization). This lesson covers methods to test for primality, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, and the distribution of primes. Understanding primes is crucial for HCF, LCM, and number theory.

lessons.title: Prime Factorization
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches how to express any composite number as a product of prime factors using factor trees and division methods.

blocks.text: 1.11 Prime Factorization

Prime factorization is the process of breaking down a composite number into a product of prime numbers. Two common methods are the factor tree and the repeated division by primes. For example, 60 = 2² × 3 × 5. This representation is unique for each number (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic). Prime factorization is essential for finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Lowest Common Multiple (LCM), and for simplifying surds and radicals.

lessons.title: Highest Common Factor (HCF)
lessons.summary: This lesson explains how to find the HCF of two or more numbers using prime factorization and the division method.

blocks.text: 1.12 Highest Common Factor (HCF)

The Highest Common Factor (HCF), also called the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD), is the largest positive integer that divides all given numbers without remainder. Two methods are taught: prime factorization (multiply the lowest powers of common primes) and the Euclidean algorithm (repeated division). HCF is used in simplifying fractions, dividing quantities into equal groups, and solving problems involving common divisors.

lessons.title: Lowest Common Multiple (LCM)
lessons.summary: This lesson demonstrates how to find the LCM of numbers using prime factorization and the division method.

blocks.text: 1.13 Lowest Common Multiple (LCM)

The Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest positive integer that is a multiple of all given numbers. It is found by prime factorization (multiply the highest powers of all primes) or by the division ladder method. LCM is essential for adding and subtracting fractions, solving problems involving repeated cycles, and finding common denominators.

lessons.title: Divisibility Rules
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches quick rules for determining divisibility by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11.

blocks.text: 1.14 Divisibility Rules

Divisibility rules help decide whether a number is divisible by another without performing long division. For example, a number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even; by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3; by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5; by 10 if it ends in 0. These rules save time in calculations, simplify prime factorization, and are useful in checking answers. This lesson covers rules for numbers 2 through 11.

lessons.title: Fractions: Understanding and Operations
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces proper, improper, and mixed fractions, and covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of fractions.

blocks.text: 1.15 Fractions: Understanding and Operations

A fraction represents a part of a whole and is written as a/b, where a is the numerator and b is the denominator (b≠0). Proper fractions have numerator < denominator; improper fractions have numerator ≥ denominator; mixed numbers combine a whole number and a fraction. This lesson teaches how to convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers, simplify fractions, and perform all four operations. Emphasis is on finding common denominators for addition/subtraction, and cancelling factors for multiplication/division.

lessons.title: Decimals and Percentages
lessons.summary: This lesson covers decimal notation, operations, and conversion between fractions, decimals, and percentages.

blocks.text: 1.16 Decimals and Percentages

Decimals are a way of writing fractions with denominators that are powers of 10. Percentages are fractions with denominator 100. This lesson covers place value in decimals, converting between fractions, decimals, and percentages, and performing operations with decimals (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division). Applications include financial calculations, measurement, and data representation. Understanding these conversions is vital for JAMB Mathematics.

lessons.title: Ratios and Proportions
lessons.summary: This lesson explains ratios as comparisons of quantities and proportions as equations of ratios, including direct and inverse proportion.

blocks.text: 1.17 Ratios and Proportions

A ratio compares two quantities of the same type (e.g., 3:2). A proportion states that two ratios are equal (e.g., a/b = c/d). This lesson covers simplifying ratios, finding equivalent ratios, and solving problems involving direct and inverse proportion. Direct proportion means as one quantity increases, the other increases at the same rate (y ∝ x). Inverse proportion means as one increases, the other decreases (y ∝ 1/x). These concepts are applied in many real-world problems.

lessons.title: Rates and Speed
lessons.summary: This lesson covers the concept of rates, including speed, distance-time calculations, and work rates.

blocks.text: 1.18 Rates and Speed

A rate compares two different quantities with different units, such as speed (distance per time), cost per item, or work rate. The basic formula for speed is speed = distance/time. This lesson teaches how to solve problems involving average speed, relative speed, and conversion between units (e.g., m/s to km/h). Work rate problems involve the amount of work done per unit time. Understanding rates is essential for motion problems and efficiency calculations.

lessons.title: Approximation and Estimation
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches rounding to decimal places and significant figures, and using estimation to check answers.

blocks.text: 1.19 Approximation and Estimation

Approximation involves rounding numbers to a given degree of accuracy, such as a certain number of decimal places or significant figures. Estimation uses rounded numbers to quickly approximate the result of a calculation, useful for checking if an answer is reasonable. This lesson covers the rules for rounding, identifying significant figures, and applying estimation to arithmetic and word problems. These skills are important for time management in examinations.

lessons.title: Standard Form (Scientific Notation)
lessons.summary: This lesson covers writing very large or very small numbers in standard form A×10^n and performing operations.

blocks.text: 1.20 Standard Form (Scientific Notation)

Standard form, or scientific notation, expresses numbers as A × 10^n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer. This is used for very large or very small numbers. The lesson teaches how to convert between ordinary and standard form, and how to multiply and divide numbers in standard form. This is essential in physics, chemistry, and engineering, and appears in JAMB questions involving large quantities like population or microscopic measurements.

lessons.title: Number Bases: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces number bases (binary, octal, decimal, hexadecimal) and place value in different bases.

blocks.text: 1.21 Number Bases: Introduction

A number base is the number of unique digits used to represent numbers. Base 10 (decimal) is most common, but other bases like binary (base 2), octal (base 8), and hexadecimal (base 16) are used in computing. This lesson explains place value in different bases, showing that each position represents a power of the base. For example, in base 2, the digits are 0 and 1, and the place values are powers of 2. Understanding bases is essential for computer science and some JAMB questions.

lessons.title: Number Bases: Conversion Between Bases
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches conversion of numbers between different bases, including from other bases to base 10 and vice versa.

blocks.text: 1.22 Number Bases: Conversion Between Bases

Conversion between bases involves expanding numbers in terms of powers of the base. To convert from another base to base 10, multiply each digit by its place value and sum. To convert from base 10 to another base, repeatedly divide by the base and record remainders. This lesson also covers direct conversion between binary and octal/hexadecimal using grouping. Mastery of these conversions is essential for solving number base problems in JAMB.

lessons.title: Number Bases: Operations
lessons.summary: This lesson covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division in number bases.

blocks.text: 1.23 Number Bases: Operations

Arithmetic operations in other bases follow the same principles as base 10, but carrying and borrowing are based on the base value. For example, in base 2, 1+1 = 10 (carry 1). This lesson teaches addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division in bases such as binary, octal, and hexadecimal. Worked examples demonstrate the step-by-step process, and practice problems help students become comfortable with operations in non-decimal bases.

lessons.title: Binary Operations
lessons.summary: This lesson defines binary operations on sets, exploring closure, commutativity, associativity, identity, and inverse properties.

blocks.text: 1.24 Binary Operations

A binary operation combines two elements from a set to produce another element. Examples include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and composition of functions. This lesson teaches how to represent an operation using a table, and how to test for properties like closure (result remains in the set), commutativity (a*b = b*a), associativity ((a*b)*c = a*(b*c)), identity element (e such that a*e = a), and inverse (a' such that a*a' = e). These properties are fundamental in abstract algebra and appear in JAMB questions.

lessons.title: Indices: Laws of Exponents
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the laws of indices (exponents) including multiplication, division, power of a power, zero, negative, and fractional indices.

blocks.text: 1.25 Indices: Laws of Exponents

Indices (or exponents) represent repeated multiplication. The laws are: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n); a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn); a^0 = 1 (a≠0); a^(-n) = 1/a^n; and a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(a^m). These laws are used to simplify algebraic expressions and solve exponential equations. This lesson provides a thorough explanation of each law with examples, and highlights common pitfalls such as confusion between (a^m)^n and a^(m^n).

lessons.title: Indices: Applications and Equations
lessons.summary: This lesson applies index laws to simplify expressions and solve exponential equations.

blocks.text: 1.26 Indices: Applications and Equations

This lesson focuses on applying the laws of indices to simplify complex algebraic expressions and solve equations where the variable appears as an exponent. Techniques include equating bases when possible, or using logarithms when bases differ. The lesson also covers exponential growth and decay problems, such as population growth and compound interest, which are common in JAMB. Students learn to manipulate indices to isolate the variable and solve for it.

lessons.title: Logarithms: Introduction and Laws
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces logarithms as the inverse of indices, covering definition and laws of logarithms.

blocks.text: 1.27 Logarithms: Introduction and Laws

A logarithm answers the question: 'To what power must the base be raised to produce a given number?' The definition is: if y = a^x, then log_a(y) = x. The laws of logarithms are derived from the laws of indices: log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y; log_a(x/y) = log_a x - log_a y; log_a(x^n) = n log_a x; and the change of base formula: log_a b = log_c b / log_c a. This lesson covers the basics and prepares students for solving logarithmic equations.

lessons.title: Logarithms: Applications and Equations
lessons.summary: This lesson applies logarithm laws to solve logarithmic and exponential equations, and to simplify calculations.

blocks.text: 1.28 Logarithms: Applications and Equations

This lesson teaches how to solve equations involving logarithms (e.g., log_a x = b) and exponential equations using logarithms. It also covers applications such as compound interest calculations, pH in chemistry, and the Richter scale for earthquakes. The change of base formula is used when bases are not compatible. Students learn to manipulate logarithmic expressions and apply them to real-world problems, which is a common JAMB topic.

lessons.title: Surds: Introduction and Simplification
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces surds as irrational roots, covering simplification of surds and operations.

blocks.text: 1.29 Surds: Introduction and Simplification

A surd is an irrational number that can be written as a root, e.g., √2, √3, ³√5. This lesson teaches how to simplify surds by factoring out perfect squares (e.g., √12 = 2√3). It also covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of surds, including the concept of rationalising the denominator (removing surds from the denominator of a fraction). Surds appear frequently in geometry (Pythagoras), trigonometry, and mensuration, making this an essential skill.

lessons.title: Surds: Equations and Applications
lessons.summary: This lesson solves equations involving surds and applies surds in geometry and mensuration.

blocks.text: 1.30 Surds: Equations and Applications

This lesson covers solving equations that contain surds, such as √(x+2) = 3. Techniques include isolating the surd, squaring both sides, and checking for extraneous solutions. It also applies surds to geometrical problems, like finding the diagonal of a square or the height of an equilateral triangle using Pythagoras' theorem. Practical examples include calculating distances and areas in radical form. Mastery of surd manipulation is crucial for JAMB.

lessons.title: Financial Mathematics
lessons.summary: This lesson covers profit, loss, discounts, commissions, simple and compound interest, depreciation, hire purchase, and taxation.

blocks.text: 1.31 Financial Mathematics

Financial mathematics applies percentages and formulas to real-life money situations. Topics include: profit/loss percentage, discount (marked price - selling price), commission (percentage of sales), simple interest (I = PRT/100), compound interest (A = P(1+R/100)^n), depreciation (reduction in value over time), hire purchase (buying on credit with interest), and taxation (income tax, VAT). This lesson provides formulas for each, explains the meaning of variables, and shows how to solve word problems. These are common JAMB questions.

lessons.title: Algebraic Expressions: Terms, Coefficients and Constants
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces algebraic expressions, defining terms, coefficients, constants, variables, and identifying like and unlike terms.

blocks.text: 2.1 Algebraic Expressions: Terms, Coefficients and Constants

Algebraic expressions are combinations of numbers, variables (letters), and arithmetic operations. A term is a product of numbers and variables; the coefficient is the numerical factor of a term; the constant is a term without a variable. Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power, and can be combined. This lesson establishes the language of algebra, essential for all subsequent algebraic manipulation.

lessons.title: Operations on Algebraic Expressions
lessons.summary: This lesson covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of algebraic expressions.

blocks.text: 2.2 Operations on Algebraic Expressions

This lesson teaches how to add and subtract algebraic expressions by combining like terms, and how to multiply and divide monomials and polynomials. Multiplication involves the distributive property, while division uses index laws. Emphasis is placed on proper handling of signs and coefficients. These skills are foundational for solving equations and simplifying complex expressions.

lessons.title: Expansion of Algebraic Expressions
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches expansion using the distributive property, including binomial products and special expansions.

blocks.text: 2.3 Expansion of Algebraic Expressions

Expansion (or removing brackets) is done by multiplying each term inside the bracket by the factor outside. Special products include (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a-b)² = a² - 2ab + b², and (a+b)(a-b) = a² - b². This lesson also covers expansion of three-term and higher-degree expressions. These expansions are essential for factorization and solving equations.

lessons.title: Factorization: Basic Methods
lessons.summary: This lesson covers factorization by common factors, grouping, and difference of squares.

blocks.text: 2.4 Factorization: Basic Methods

Factorization is the reverse of expansion: writing an expression as a product of its factors. Basic methods include taking out the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of all terms, grouping terms to reveal common factors, and using the difference of squares formula a² - b² = (a-b)(a+b). This lesson provides step-by-step examples and emphasizes identifying patterns. Factorization is key to solving quadratic equations and simplifying algebraic fractions.

lessons.title: Factorization: Advanced Methods
lessons.summary: This lesson covers factorization of quadratic trinomials, sum/difference of cubes, and use of algebraic identities.

blocks.text: 2.5 Factorization: Advanced Methods

Advanced factorization includes trinomials of the form ax² + bx + c, perfect square trinomials, and sum/difference of cubes (a³±b³). Techniques such as splitting the middle term, completing the square, and substitution are explored. This lesson also covers factorization using identities like (a+b+c)² and applications in solving polynomial equations. Mastery of these methods is crucial for higher-level algebra in JAMB.

lessons.title: Algebraic Fractions
lessons.summary: This lesson covers simplification, addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of algebraic fractions.

blocks.text: 2.6 Algebraic Fractions

Algebraic fractions have variables in the numerator and/or denominator. Simplification is done by factoring and cancelling common factors. Addition and subtraction require finding a common denominator (LCM of denominators). Multiplication is straightforward (multiply numerators and denominators), while division involves multiplying by the reciprocal. This lesson also covers complex fractions (fractions within fractions). These skills are essential for solving equations with fractions.

lessons.title: Substitution in Algebraic Expressions
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches evaluating algebraic expressions by substituting numerical values for variables.

blocks.text: 2.7 Substitution in Algebraic Expressions

Substitution involves replacing variables with given numbers and simplifying using the order of operations (BODMAS/PEMDAS). This skill is used in evaluating formulas, checking solutions to equations, and solving word problems. This lesson provides many examples with different types of expressions (polynomials, fractions, roots) and emphasizes careful handling of negative numbers and brackets.

lessons.title: Change of Subject of Formula
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches rearranging formulas to make a different variable the subject using inverse operations.

blocks.text: 2.8 Change of Subject of Formula

Given a formula like A = πr², we may need to solve for r. This involves applying inverse operations to isolate the desired variable. This lesson covers formulas with linear, quadratic, and rational terms, and demonstrates the steps: identify the variable, perform inverse operations in reverse order, and simplify. This skill is vital in physics, geometry, and financial mathematics, and is a common JAMB question type.

lessons.title: Linear Equations in One Variable
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches solving linear equations of the form ax+b=c, including those with brackets and fractions.

blocks.text: 2.9 Linear Equations in One Variable

A linear equation in one variable has the variable to the first power. The goal is to isolate the variable on one side. Steps include: expanding brackets, collecting like terms, and using inverse operations (addition/subtraction, multiplication/division). Equations with fractions require multiplying by the LCD. This lesson includes verification by substituting the solution. These are the simplest equations and form the basis for more complex ones.

lessons.title: Linear Equations in Two Variables
lessons.summary: This lesson covers linear equations in two variables, graphing them, and understanding their solutions.

blocks.text: 2.10 Linear Equations in Two Variables

A linear equation in two variables (x and y) has the general form ax + by = c. It has infinitely many solutions (ordered pairs) that lie on a straight line. This lesson covers finding intercepts, plotting points, and graphing the line. It also introduces the concept of slope (gradient) and the different forms of the equation. Understanding two-variable equations is essential for simultaneous equations and coordinate geometry.

lessons.title: Simultaneous Equations: Elimination Method
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches solving two linear equations simultaneously by eliminating one variable.

blocks.text: 2.11 Simultaneous Equations: Elimination Method

The elimination method involves adding or subtracting the equations to cancel one variable, allowing solution for the other. Steps: align variables, multiply equations if necessary to get equal coefficients for one variable, then add/subtract to eliminate. The resulting single-variable equation is solved, then substituted back to find the other variable. This method is efficient when coefficients are easy to manipulate and is widely used in JAMB.

lessons.title: Simultaneous Equations: Substitution Method
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches solving simultaneous equations by substituting one equation into the other.

blocks.text: 2.12 Simultaneous Equations: Substitution Method

The substitution method involves solving one equation for one variable and substituting that expression into the other equation. This reduces the system to a single equation in one variable. After solving, the result is substituted back to find the other variable. This method is particularly useful when one variable has coefficient 1 or -1. Both elimination and substitution methods are important; the choice depends on the equations.

lessons.title: Simultaneous Equations: Word Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson applies simultaneous equations to solve real-world word problems.

blocks.text: 2.13 Simultaneous Equations: Word Problems

Many practical problems involve two unknown quantities that can be represented by two variables. This lesson teaches how to translate a word problem into a system of linear equations, solve it, and interpret the solution in context. Examples include age problems, mixture problems, cost problems, and motion problems. Students learn to identify the unknowns, form equations from the given relationships, and solve using the appropriate method.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces quadratic equations in standard form ax²+bx+c=0 and their components.

blocks.text: 2.14 Quadratic Equations: Introduction

A quadratic equation is a polynomial equation of degree 2. The standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, and c are constants and a ≠ 0. This lesson explains how to identify a, b, c, and the number of possible solutions (up to two real roots). The shape of the graph (parabola) is introduced, linking algebra to geometry. This foundational lesson prepares students for the various methods of solving quadratics.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations: Solving by Factorization
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches solving quadratics by factoring the expression and setting each factor to zero.

blocks.text: 2.15 Quadratic Equations: Solving by Factorization

If a quadratic expression can be factored into two linear factors, setting each factor to zero (zero product property) gives the solutions. This method requires that the quadratic be in standard form and factorable. The lesson covers factoring techniques (common factor, trinomials, difference of squares) and provides many examples. Factorization is often the quickest method when the roots are rational numbers.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations: Completing the Square
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches solving quadratics by completing the square, a method that leads to the quadratic formula.

blocks.text: 2.16 Quadratic Equations: Completing the Square

Completing the square transforms a quadratic expression into a perfect square plus or minus a constant. Steps: ensure coefficient of x² is 1, move constant to RHS, add (b/2)² to both sides, then factor the LHS as a square. This method yields solutions by taking square roots. It is essential for deriving the quadratic formula and for solving quadratics that are not easily factorable. It also helps in graphing parabolas.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations: The Quadratic Formula
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces and applies the quadratic formula x = (-b ± √(b²-4ac))/2a.

blocks.text: 2.17 Quadratic Equations: The Quadratic Formula

The quadratic formula is a universal method that solves any quadratic equation in standard form. It is derived by completing the square. The formula is x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / (2a). This lesson emphasizes correct substitution of a, b, c, simplification of the discriminant, and interpreting the solutions. It also discusses the case when the discriminant is negative (no real roots). The formula is a powerful tool that JAMB students must master.

lessons.title: The Discriminant and Nature of Roots
lessons.summary: This lesson explores the discriminant Δ=b²-4ac to determine the nature of roots (real, equal, or complex).

blocks.text: 2.18 The Discriminant and Nature of Roots

The discriminant Δ = b² - 4ac provides information about the roots of a quadratic equation without solving it. If Δ > 0, there are two distinct real roots; if Δ = 0, one repeated real root; if Δ < 0, no real roots (complex conjugate). This lesson also connects the discriminant to the graph of the parabola (number of x-intercepts). Understanding the discriminant is crucial for solving problems that ask for conditions on a, b, c.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations: Word Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson applies quadratic equations to solve word problems, including area, motion, and number problems.

blocks.text: 2.19 Quadratic Equations: Word Problems

Many real-life situations lead to quadratic equations, such as finding dimensions of a rectangle given area and perimeter, projectile motion, and number puzzles. This lesson teaches how to translate a word problem into a quadratic equation, solve it, and select the valid solution (discarding negative or non-realistic roots). Emphasis is on setting up the equation correctly and interpreting the answer in context.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations: Graphical Interpretation
lessons.summary: This lesson covers graphing quadratic functions, identifying vertex, axis of symmetry, and intercepts.

blocks.text: 2.20 Quadratic Equations: Graphical Interpretation

The graph of a quadratic function y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola. This lesson teaches how to find the vertex (turning point), axis of symmetry (x = -b/2a), y-intercept (c), and x-intercepts (roots). The effect of the coefficient 'a' on the shape (opening upward/downward) and width is discussed. Graphical interpretation is useful for visualizing solutions to quadratic inequalities and understanding the relationship between the discriminant and graph.

lessons.title: Linear Inequalities
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches solving linear inequalities and representing solutions on a number line.

blocks.text: 2.21 Linear Inequalities

Inequalities compare two expressions using <, >, ≤, or ≥. Solving linear inequalities is similar to solving equations, except that multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. The solution is often an interval on the number line. This lesson covers both one-variable and two-variable inequalities (graphs of half-planes). Understanding inequalities is essential for solving systems and for real-world constraints.

lessons.title: Quadratic Inequalities
lessons.summary: This lesson solves quadratic inequalities using sign analysis and graphical methods.

blocks.text: 2.22 Quadratic Inequalities

Quadratic inequalities like ax² + bx + c > 0 are solved by finding the roots and determining the sign of the quadratic in intervals. Methods include factorization and the sign chart, or graphing the parabola and identifying intervals where it lies above or below the x-axis. This lesson covers both methods and handles strict vs. non-strict inequalities. These are common in JAMB and require careful handling.

lessons.title: Variation: Direct Variation
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces direct variation y∝x, finding the constant of variation, and solving problems.

blocks.text: 2.23 Variation: Direct Variation

Direct variation means two quantities change in the same ratio: y = kx, where k is the constant of variation. This lesson covers finding k from given values, then using the relationship to find unknown quantities. Problems include areas, volumes, and simple proportionality. Direct variation is a common theme in JAMB word problems, especially in physics and geometry.

lessons.title: Variation: Inverse Variation
lessons.summary: This lesson covers inverse variation y∝1/x, with constant of variation and problem solving.

blocks.text: 2.24 Variation: Inverse Variation

Inverse variation occurs when one quantity increases while the other decreases: y = k/x. This lesson teaches finding k and using the relationship to solve problems such as speed vs. time, work rate, and gas pressure. Emphasis is on understanding the inverse relationship and setting up the equation correctly. Both direct and inverse variation are tested in JAMB.

lessons.title: Variation: Joint and Partial Variation
lessons.summary: This lesson explores joint variation (y∝xz) and partial variation (y = a + bx).

blocks.text: 2.25 Variation: Joint and Partial Variation

Joint variation involves a variable varying directly as the product of two or more variables (e.g., y = kxz). Partial variation combines a constant term and a variable term (e.g., y = a + bx). This lesson teaches how to find the constants (k, a, b) using given conditions and solve problems. These types of variation appear in advanced JAMB questions and require careful algebraic manipulation.

lessons.title: Sequences: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces sequences as ordered lists of numbers, with general term notation.

blocks.text: 2.26 Sequences: Introduction

A sequence is a function whose domain is the set of positive integers. Each term is denoted by a_n, where n is the position. This lesson covers how to find a term given a formula, how to generate terms from a recurrence relation, and how to identify patterns. Sequences are the foundation for series and progressions, which are common JAMB topics.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Progression (AP)
lessons.summary: This lesson covers AP: definition, nth term formula, and sum of n terms.

blocks.text: 2.27 Arithmetic Progression (AP)

An Arithmetic Progression (AP) is a sequence where the difference between consecutive terms is constant (common difference, d). Formulas: nth term a_n = a + (n-1)d; sum of first n terms S_n = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d] = n/2 (a + l), where l is last term. This lesson teaches how to find terms, sums, and solve problems involving AP. APs are frequently used in JAMB for age, salary, and other linear growth problems.

lessons.title: Geometric Progression (GP)
lessons.summary: This lesson covers GP: definition, nth term, sum of n terms, and sum to infinity.

blocks.text: 2.28 Geometric Progression (GP)

A Geometric Progression (GP) has a constant ratio (r) between consecutive terms. Formulas: nth term a_n = ar^(n-1); sum of first n terms S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) for r ≠ 1; sum to infinity S_∞ = a/(1 - r) for |r| < 1. This lesson covers all aspects, including finding terms, sums, and solving problems involving growth, depreciation, and recurring patterns.

lessons.title: Sequences: Applications and Sum to Infinity
lessons.summary: This lesson applies AP and GP to word problems and explores sum to infinity of GP.

blocks.text: 2.29 Sequences: Applications and Sum to Infinity

This lesson applies AP and GP to real-world scenarios such as population growth, loan repayments, and depreciation. It also covers the sum to infinity of a convergent GP, which is useful for infinite processes. Students learn to model situations with sequences and solve for unknowns. These applications are common in JAMB and require translating word problems into sequence notation.

lessons.title: Matrices: Introduction and Operations
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces matrices, order, addition, subtraction, and scalar multiplication.

blocks.text: 2.30 Matrices: Introduction and Operations

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. The order is m×n (rows × columns). This lesson covers basic operations: addition and subtraction (same order), and multiplication by a scalar. It also introduces notation and types of matrices (row, column, square, zero, identity). Matrices are used to solve systems of equations and are tested in JAMB.

lessons.title: Matrices: Multiplication
lessons.summary: This lesson covers matrix multiplication, including conditions and the row-column method.

blocks.text: 2.31 Matrices: Multiplication

Matrix multiplication is defined when the number of columns of the first matrix equals the number of rows of the second. The product is obtained by multiplying rows of the first by columns of the second and summing. This lesson covers the mechanics and provides examples. It also introduces the concept of the identity matrix and how multiplication works. Matrix multiplication is a key topic in JAMB.

lessons.title: Matrices: Determinants and Inverses
lessons.summary: This lesson covers determinants of 2×2 matrices and finding inverses to solve linear systems.

blocks.text: 2.32 Matrices: Determinants and Inverses

For a 2×2 matrix A = [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad - bc. If det(A) ≠ 0, the inverse exists: A⁻¹ = (1/det) [[d, -b], [-c, a]]. This lesson covers calculation of determinant and inverse, and uses them to solve simultaneous equations (AX = B ⇒ X = A⁻¹B). Understanding determinants and inverses is essential for advanced algebra and JAMB problems.

lessons.title: Sets: Introduction and Notation
lessons.summary: This lesson defines sets, elements, and set-builder/roster notation, including universal and empty sets.

blocks.text: 3.1 Sets: Introduction and Notation

A set is a collection of distinct objects, called elements. Notation includes roster (listing elements) and set-builder (describing properties). Special sets: universal set (U), empty set (∅), finite/infinite sets. This lesson covers membership (∈), subset (⊆), and proper subset (⊂). Understanding set notation is crucial for Venn diagrams and probability.

lessons.title: Sets: Union and Intersection
lessons.summary: This lesson covers union (∪) and intersection (∩) of sets, with properties and examples.

blocks.text: 3.2 Sets: Union and Intersection

The union of two sets A and B (A∪B) is the set of elements in A or B (or both). The intersection (A∩B) contains elements in both A and B. This lesson teaches how to find these operations and their properties (commutative, associative, distributive). Venn diagrams are introduced as a visual aid. These operations are foundational for solving problems involving multiple sets.

lessons.title: Sets: Complement and Difference
lessons.summary: This lesson covers complement (A') and set difference (A-B), with notation and applications.

blocks.text: 3.3 Sets: Complement and Difference

The complement of set A (relative to U) is the set of all elements not in A (denoted A' or A^c). Set difference A - B contains elements in A but not in B. This lesson covers notation and the relationship between complement, union, and intersection. De Morgan's laws are introduced: (A∪B)' = A'∩B' and (A∩B)' = A'∪B'. These are essential for simplifying set expressions.

lessons.title: Venn Diagrams: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces Venn diagrams as visual representations of sets and their operations.

blocks.text: 3.4 Venn Diagrams: Introduction

Venn diagrams use overlapping circles to represent sets. Each region corresponds to a combination of set memberships. This lesson teaches how to draw and interpret diagrams for two or three sets, and how to shade regions corresponding to various operations (union, intersection, complement, difference). Venn diagrams are a powerful tool for solving set problems and are frequently used in JAMB.

lessons.title: Venn Diagrams: Two-Set Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson solves problems involving two sets using Venn diagrams and cardinalities.

blocks.text: 3.5 Venn Diagrams: Two-Set Problems

Given information about the total number of elements, and the numbers in each set and their intersection, we can fill in the regions of a two-set Venn diagram. This lesson teaches how to find unknown cardinalities by using the principle of inclusion-exclusion: |A∪B| = |A| + |B| - |A∩B|. Practical examples include surveys and classification problems.

lessons.title: Venn Diagrams: Three-Set Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson extends Venn diagrams to three sets, solving problems with up to eight regions.

blocks.text: 3.6 Venn Diagrams: Three-Set Problems

Three overlapping sets divide the universal set into up to 8 regions. This lesson teaches systematic filling of regions starting from the intersection of all three sets, then intersections of pairs, then the individual sets, and finally the outside. The inclusion-exclusion principle for three sets is covered: |A∪B∪C| = |A| + |B| + |C| - |A∩B| - |A∩C| - |B∩C| + |A∩B∩C|. These problems are common in JAMB.

lessons.title: Sets: Word Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson focuses on translating word problems into set notation and Venn diagrams.

blocks.text: 3.7 Sets: Word Problems

Many real-world problems can be modelled using sets, e.g., surveying people with preferences, or categorizing objects. This lesson teaches how to read a word problem, identify the sets and their relationships, construct a Venn diagram, and use it to find the required quantities. Emphasis is on careful reading and systematic diagramming. This is a high-frequency JAMB topic.

lessons.title: Sets: Properties and Laws
lessons.summary: This lesson summarizes properties of set operations, including De Morgan's laws and distributive laws.

blocks.text: 3.8 Sets: Properties and Laws

This lesson consolidates the commutative, associative, distributive, identity, and complement laws for set operations. It also covers De Morgan's laws in detail and the inclusion-exclusion principle for two and three sets. These laws are used to simplify complex set expressions and to prove set identities. Understanding these properties is crucial for advanced set problems and logical reasoning.

lessons.title: Points, Lines and Planes
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the undefined terms of geometry: points, lines, line segments, rays, and planes.

blocks.text: 4.1 Points, Lines and Planes

Geometry begins with three undefined terms: point (no dimension), line (infinite length), and plane (flat surface). This lesson covers notation for points, lines, segments, and rays. It also discusses collinearity, coplanarity, and basic postulates (e.g., through any two points there is exactly one line). These concepts form the foundation for all geometric reasoning.

lessons.title: Angles: Types and Measurement
lessons.summary: This lesson defines angles, classifies them (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex), and covers measurement.

blocks.text: 4.2 Angles: Types and Measurement

An angle is formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint. Angles are measured in degrees. Types: acute (<90°), right (90°), obtuse (90°–180°), straight (180°), reflex (180°–360°). This lesson also covers complementary angles (sum 90°) and supplementary angles (sum 180°). Understanding angle classification is essential for solving geometric problems.

lessons.title: Angles and Parallel Lines
lessons.summary: This lesson explores angles formed when a transversal intersects parallel lines.

blocks.text: 4.3 Angles and Parallel Lines

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, specific angle relationships hold: corresponding angles are equal; alternate interior angles are equal; alternate exterior angles are equal; co-interior (same-side interior) angles sum to 180°. This lesson teaches how to identify these angle pairs and use them to find unknown angles. These properties are fundamental in geometric proofs.

lessons.title: Triangles: Introduction and Classification
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces triangles, classifying by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse).

blocks.text: 4.4 Triangles: Introduction and Classification

A triangle has three sides and three angles, summing to 180°. Classification by sides: equilateral (all equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (no equal). Classification by angles: acute (all <90°), right (one 90°), obtuse (one >90°). This lesson also covers the exterior angle theorem (exterior angle equals sum of two opposite interior angles). Triangles are the building blocks of many geometric figures.

lessons.title: Triangles: Congruence and Similarity
lessons.summary: This lesson covers conditions for congruent (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and similar (AA, SSS, SAS) triangles.

blocks.text: 4.5 Triangles: Congruence and Similarity

Congruent triangles are identical in shape and size. Conditions: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and included angle), ASA (two angles and included side), RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, side). Similar triangles have same shape but different size; conditions: AA (two angles), SSS (sides proportional), SAS (two sides proportional and included angle equal). This lesson teaches how to prove triangles congruent/similar and use them to find unknown lengths.

lessons.title: Pythagoras' Theorem
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces Pythagoras' theorem a²+b²=c² for right-angled triangles and its converse.

blocks.text: 4.6 Pythagoras' Theorem

In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (side opposite right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a² + b² = c². The converse states that if a² + b² = c², then the triangle is right-angled. This lesson covers finding missing sides, and applications in geometry, coordinate geometry, and trigonometry. Pythagoras' theorem is a cornerstone of JAMB Mathematics.

lessons.title: Quadrilaterals: Types and Properties
lessons.summary: This lesson covers the properties of quadrilaterals: square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium, and kite.

blocks.text: 4.7 Quadrilaterals: Types and Properties

A quadrilateral is a four-sided polygon. Sum of interior angles = 360°. Key types: square (four equal sides, right angles), rectangle (opposite sides equal, right angles), parallelogram (opposite sides parallel and equal), rhombus (all sides equal, opposite angles equal), trapezium (one pair of parallel sides), kite (two pairs of adjacent equal sides). This lesson details each shape's properties, including diagonals and symmetry.

lessons.title: Polygons: Interior and Exterior Angles
lessons.summary: This lesson explores polygons, with formulas for sum of interior angles and exterior angles.

blocks.text: 4.8 Polygons: Interior and Exterior Angles

A polygon is a closed figure with straight sides. Sum of interior angles = (n-2)×180°, where n is the number of sides. Each interior angle of a regular polygon = (n-2)×180°/n. The sum of exterior angles is always 360°. This lesson covers regular vs. irregular polygons and solving for unknown angles. Polygons appear in many geometry and mensuration problems.

lessons.title: Circles: Introduction and Basic Properties
lessons.summary: This lesson defines circle parts: centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc, sector, segment, tangent, and secant.

blocks.text: 4.9 Circles: Introduction and Basic Properties

A circle is a set of points equidistant from a fixed centre. Key parts: radius (centre to circumference), diameter (twice radius), chord (line segment joining two points on circle), arc (portion of circumference), sector (region bounded by two radii and an arc), segment (region bounded by chord and arc), tangent (line touching circle at one point), secant (line intersecting circle at two points). This lesson defines and illustrates each.

lessons.title: Circle Theorems: Angle at Centre
lessons.summary: This lesson proves and applies the theorem: angle at centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

blocks.text: 4.10 Circle Theorems: Angle at Centre

The theorem states: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre of the circle is twice the angle subtended at the circumference (at any point on the remaining arc). This lesson provides a proof using isosceles triangles formed by radii and a chord. Applications include finding unknown angles and proving other circle theorems. This is one of the most important circle theorems in JAMB.

lessons.title: Circle Theorems: Angles in the Same Segment
lessons.summary: This lesson covers the theorem: angles in the same segment are equal.

blocks.text: 4.11 Circle Theorems: Angles in the Same Segment

If two angles are subtended by the same chord at the circumference, and their vertices lie on the same side of the chord, then the angles are equal. This theorem is a direct consequence of the angle at centre theorem. This lesson provides proof and examples of using it to find unknown angles in circles. It is frequently used in combination with other circle theorems.

lessons.title: Circle Theorems: Angle in a Semicircle
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle (90°).

blocks.text: 4.12 Circle Theorems: Angle in a Semicircle

The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference is 90°. This is a special case of the angle at centre theorem: the angle at centre for a diameter is 180°, so the angle at circumference is half that, i.e., 90°. This theorem is widely used in geometry, trigonometry, and mensuration problems involving circles and right triangles.

lessons.title: Circle Theorems: Cyclic Quadrilaterals
lessons.summary: This lesson covers the property: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.

blocks.text: 4.13 Circle Theorems: Cyclic Quadrilaterals

A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral whose vertices all lie on a circle. The theorem states that opposite angles are supplementary (sum to 180°). This lesson proves the theorem using the angle at centre theorem. It also covers the converse: if opposite angles of a quadrilateral sum to 180°, then it is cyclic. This property is useful in solving geometry problems.

lessons.title: Circle Theorems: Tangent Properties
lessons.summary: This lesson explores tangent properties: radius perpendicular to tangent, equal tangents from external point, and alternate segment theorem.

blocks.text: 4.14 Circle Theorems: Tangent Properties

Important tangent properties: (1) The radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent. (2) Tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length. (3) The alternate segment theorem (tangent-chord theorem) states that the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. This lesson covers these with proofs and examples, essential for JAMB geometry.

lessons.title: Circle Theorems: Combined Applications
lessons.summary: This lesson solves complex problems combining multiple circle theorems.

blocks.text: 4.15 Circle Theorems: Combined Applications

Many JAMB problems require using several circle theorems in a single problem. This lesson provides step-by-step strategies: identify the relevant theorems, set up relationships, and solve for unknowns. Examples include problems with multiple chords, tangents, and intersecting lines. Students learn to recognize which theorem applies in a given configuration. Mastery of combined applications is key to high scores.

lessons.title: Geometric Constructions
lessons.summary: This lesson covers constructions using compass and straightedge: angle bisector, perpendicular bisector, triangles.

blocks.text: 4.16 Geometric Constructions

Constructions are exact drawings using only a compass and straightedge (unmarked ruler). This lesson teaches how to construct: angle bisector, perpendicular bisector of a segment, perpendicular to a line from a point, and triangles from given data (SSS, SAS, ASA). Step-by-step instructions and diagrams are provided. Constructions test understanding of geometric properties and are sometimes examined in JAMB.

lessons.title: Loci
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces loci: sets of points satisfying a condition, including circles, perpendicular bisectors, and angle bisectors.

blocks.text: 4.17 Loci

A locus is a set of points that satisfy a given condition. This lesson covers the locus of points: (a) at a fixed distance from a point (circle), (b) equidistant from two points (perpendicular bisector), (c) equidistant from two lines (angle bisectors), (d) at a fixed distance from a line (parallel lines). Understanding loci helps in solving construction problems and geometry proofs. Loci questions appear in JAMB.

lessons.title: Bearings
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches three-figure bearings and solving problems involving bearings.

blocks.text: 4.18 Bearings

A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north, expressed as a three-digit number (e.g., 045° for north-east). This lesson covers how to measure and draw bearings, and how to use them in navigation problems. It also includes converting between bearings and compass directions, and solving problems involving distances and bearings using trigonometry. Bearings are common in JAMB and require careful interpretation.

lessons.title: Geometry: Word Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson applies geometric concepts to solve word problems involving shapes, angles, and theorems.

blocks.text: 4.19 Geometry: Word Problems

Geometry word problems require translating a real-world situation into a geometric diagram, then using properties and theorems to find unknowns. This lesson covers problems involving angles, parallel lines, triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and bearings. Emphasis is on drawing accurate diagrams and applying the correct theorems. Students practice multi-step problems that integrate several concepts.

lessons.title: Geometry: JAMB Focus and Common Errors
lessons.summary: This lesson consolidates geometry topics with JAMB-style questions and highlights common mistakes.

blocks.text: 4.20 Geometry: JAMB Focus and Common Errors

This final geometry lesson reviews key concepts and presents typical JAMB-style multiple-choice questions. It also discusses common errors: misidentifying angles, using the wrong circle theorem, confusing congruence with similarity, and sign mistakes in coordinate geometry. Strategies for eliminating distractors and checking answers are provided. This lesson prepares students for the geometry section of the JAMB examination.

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson defines perimeter and area, introducing units and basic formulas.

blocks.text: 5.1 Perimeter and Area: Introduction

Perimeter is the total distance around a 2D shape. Area is the amount of space enclosed within the shape. Units: perimeter in mm, cm, m, km; area in mm², cm², m², etc. This lesson explains the difference between 2D and 3D measurements and provides an overview of formulas for common shapes. Understanding these concepts is essential for solving mensuration problems.

lessons.title: Area of Rectangles and Squares
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches area formulas for rectangles (A=lw) and squares (A=s²).

blocks.text: 5.2 Area of Rectangles and Squares

Area of a rectangle = length × width; area of a square = side × side. This lesson covers calculations, unit conversions (e.g., converting cm² to m²), and applications like finding the amount of paint needed for a wall or the area of a garden. Emphasis is on identifying the correct dimensions and handling units appropriately.

lessons.title: Area of Triangles and Parallelograms
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches area formulas: triangle (½×base×height) and parallelogram (base×height).

blocks.text: 5.3 Area of Triangles and Parallelograms

Area of a triangle = ½ × base × perpendicular height. Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height. This lesson covers how to identify the base and height in different orientations, and includes examples with decimals and fractions. Applications include finding the area of composite shapes and solving problems involving land measurements.

lessons.title: Area of Trapezium and Rhombus
lessons.summary: This lesson covers area of trapezium (½(a+b)h) and rhombus (½ d₁d₂).

blocks.text: 5.4 Area of Trapezium and Rhombus

Area of trapezium = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height. Area of rhombus = ½ × product of diagonals. This lesson also covers the area of a kite (same formula as rhombus) and provides examples with diagrams. These shapes often appear in composite figures, and the formulas are tested in JAMB.

lessons.title: Circumference and Area of Circle
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches circumference (C=2πr) and area (A=πr²) of a circle.

blocks.text: 5.5 Circumference and Area of Circle

Circumference = 2πr or πd; area = πr². This lesson uses π ≈ 3.142 or 22/7. It covers handling radius vs. diameter, and applications such as finding the distance around a circular track or the area of a circular garden. The relationship between circumference and diameter is emphasized, and examples include semi-circles and quarter-circles.

lessons.title: Arc Length and Sector Area
lessons.summary: This lesson covers arc length (l=θ/360×2πr) and sector area (A=θ/360×πr²).

blocks.text: 5.6 Arc Length and Sector Area

For a sector with central angle θ (in degrees), arc length = (θ/360)×2πr, and sector area = (θ/360)×πr². This lesson includes examples with different angles, and also covers problems involving segments (sector minus triangle). Applications include calculating the length of a railway track curve or the area of a slice of pizza.

lessons.title: Composite Plane Figures
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches how to find perimeters and areas of composite shapes by decomposition.

blocks.text: 5.7 Composite Plane Figures

Composite figures are made up of two or more simple shapes. To find area, decompose into rectangles, triangles, circles, etc., calculate each, and add or subtract as needed. Perimeter is found by summing the lengths of the outer edges. This lesson provides many worked examples with diagrams, including shapes with holes (subtracting areas).

lessons.title: Volume of Cube and Cuboid
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches volume formulas: cube (V=s³) and cuboid (V=lwh).

blocks.text: 5.8 Volume of Cube and Cuboid

Volume measures the amount of space occupied by a 3D shape. Cube: V = s³; cuboid: V = l × w × h. This lesson covers unit conversion (cm³ to m³, etc.) and applications like capacity of a container or volume of a room. It also discusses the difference between volume and capacity (litres).

lessons.title: Surface Area of Cube and Cuboid
lessons.summary: This lesson covers total surface area: cube (6s²) and cuboid (2(lw+lh+wh)).

blocks.text: 5.9 Surface Area of Cube and Cuboid

Surface area is the sum of the areas of all faces. Cube: SA = 6s²; cuboid: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh). This lesson also covers finding the area of an open box (no top) or a room's walls. Applications include painting, packaging, and material estimation.

lessons.title: Volume and Surface Area of Cylinder
lessons.summary: This lesson covers cylinder volume (V=πr²h) and total surface area (2πr²+2πrh).

blocks.text: 5.10 Volume and Surface Area of Cylinder

Volume of a cylinder = πr²h (area of base × height). Curved surface area = 2πrh; total surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh. This lesson includes examples of hollow cylinders (e.g., pipes) and applications like containers, tanks, and rollers.

lessons.title: Volume and Surface Area of Cone
lessons.summary: This lesson covers cone volume (V=⅓πr²h) and surface area (πr²+πrl).

blocks.text: 5.11 Volume and Surface Area of Cone

Volume of a cone = ⅓πr²h. Slant height l = √(r²+h²). Curved surface area = πrl; total surface area = πr² + πrl. This lesson covers cones of different dimensions, and applications like conical containers, tents, and funnels. The relationship between volume of cone and cylinder (⅓) is highlighted.

lessons.title: Volume and Surface Area of Sphere and Hemisphere
lessons.summary: This lesson covers sphere volume (V=⁴⁄₃πr³) and surface area (4πr²), and hemisphere formulas.

blocks.text: 5.12 Volume and Surface Area of Sphere and Hemisphere

Sphere: V = ⁴⁄₃πr³, SA = 4πr². Hemisphere: V = ⅔πr³, curved SA = 2πr², total SA = 3πr² (including the circular base). This lesson includes examples of solid spheres, hollow spheres (shells), and hemispherical bowls. Applications include balloons, planets, and domes.

lessons.title: Volume of Prism and Pyramid
lessons.summary: This lesson covers volume of prisms (base area × height) and pyramids (⅓ base area × height).

blocks.text: 5.13 Volume of Prism and Pyramid

A prism has a uniform cross-section; volume = area of base × height. A pyramid has a base and an apex; volume = ⅓ × area of base × height. This lesson covers triangular, rectangular, and other polygonal bases. It also includes examples of combined solids and frustum (truncated pyramid) where appropriate.

lessons.title: Composite Solids and Unit Conversion
lessons.summary: This lesson covers volume of composite solids and conversion between units of area and volume.

blocks.text: 5.14 Composite Solids and Unit Conversion

Composite solids are formed by combining basic shapes (e.g., cylinder with a hemisphere on top). Volume is found by summing volumes of components; surface area is sum of exposed surfaces. This lesson also covers converting between different units of area and volume (e.g., m² to cm², m³ to cm³, litres to m³). These skills are essential for practical measurement problems in JAMB.

lessons.title: The Cartesian Plane
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the Cartesian coordinate system with axes, origin, quadrants, and plotting points.

blocks.text: 6.1 The Cartesian Plane

The Cartesian plane uses two perpendicular number lines: the x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical). Their intersection is the origin (0,0). The plane is divided into four quadrants. Points are represented by ordered pairs (x,y). This lesson teaches how to plot points and identify their coordinates, and how to read coordinates from a graph.

lessons.title: Midpoint and Distance Between Points
lessons.summary: This lesson covers midpoint formula and distance formula between two points.

blocks.text: 6.2 Midpoint and Distance Between Points

The midpoint of a segment with endpoints (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2). The distance between them is √[(x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²]. This lesson provides derivations and examples, including finding midpoints and distances in geometric shapes. These formulas are fundamental in coordinate geometry.

lessons.title: Gradient (Slope) of a Line
lessons.summary: This lesson defines gradient m = (y₂-y₁)/(x₂-x₁), including positive, negative, zero, and undefined.

blocks.text: 6.3 Gradient (Slope) of a Line

The gradient (or slope) measures the steepness of a line: m = (change in y)/(change in x). Positive gradient: line rises; negative: falls; zero: horizontal; undefined: vertical. This lesson covers calculation from coordinates, and interpreting gradient in real-world contexts (e.g., speed). Gradient is essential for equations of lines.

lessons.title: Equation of a Straight Line: Point-Gradient Form
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches the point-gradient form: y - y₁ = m(x - x₁).

blocks.text: 6.4 Equation of a Straight Line: Point-Gradient Form

Given a point (x₁,y₁) and gradient m, the equation is y - y₁ = m(x - x₁). This lesson shows how to use this form to find the equation of a line, and how to convert it to other forms. This is useful when a point and slope are known, and is frequently tested in JAMB.

lessons.title: Equation of a Straight Line: Gradient-Intercept Form
lessons.summary: This lesson covers y = mx + c, identifying gradient m and y-intercept c.

blocks.text: 6.5 Equation of a Straight Line: Gradient-Intercept Form

The gradient-intercept form is y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept (the point where the line crosses the y-axis). This lesson teaches how to find m and c from a graph, from two points, or from a word problem. It also covers graphing a line from its equation.

lessons.title: Equation of a Straight Line: General Form
lessons.summary: This lesson covers the general form ax + by + c = 0 and conversion between forms.

blocks.text: 6.6 Equation of a Straight Line: General Form

The general form is ax + by + c = 0. Any linear equation can be written in this form. This lesson teaches conversion between general, gradient-intercept, and point-gradient forms. It also explains how to find gradient and intercepts from the general form. This is useful for solving systems and for applying algebraic techniques.

lessons.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches conditions: parallel (m₁=m₂) and perpendicular (m₁×m₂=-1).

blocks.text: 6.7 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

Two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient. They are perpendicular if the product of their gradients is -1 (i.e., m₁ = -1/m₂). This lesson covers how to find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line, passing through a given point. These concepts are important in geometry and coordinate geometry.

lessons.title: Intercepts of a Line
lessons.summary: This lesson covers x-intercepts and y-intercepts, and finding them from equations.

blocks.text: 6.8 Intercepts of a Line

The x-intercept is where the line crosses the x-axis (y=0). The y-intercept is where it crosses the y-axis (x=0). This lesson teaches how to find intercepts from the equation of a line, and how to use intercepts to sketch the line quickly. Intercepts are also used in the intercept form of the equation: x/a + y/b = 1.

lessons.title: Coordinate Geometry: Word Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson solves word problems using distance, midpoint, gradient, and line equations.

blocks.text: 6.9 Coordinate Geometry: Word Problems

This lesson applies coordinate geometry to practical problems: finding distances between two points, finding the midpoint of a segment, determining if lines are parallel or perpendicular, and finding equations of lines through given points. Examples include geometry problems (e.g., proving shapes) and real-world problems (e.g., finding the shortest distance).

lessons.title: Coordinate Geometry: Graphical Applications
lessons.summary: This lesson covers finding intersections of lines, and using graphs to solve systems.

blocks.text: 6.10 Coordinate Geometry: Graphical Applications

This lesson demonstrates solving two linear equations graphically by plotting both lines and finding their intersection point. It also covers using graphs to interpret data, finding the equation of a line from a graph, and applications in physics (e.g., distance-time graphs). These skills are essential for JAMB and for understanding relationships between variables.

lessons.title: Right-Angled Triangles and Basic Ratios
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces right-angled triangles and the definitions of opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse.

blocks.text: 7.1 Right-Angled Triangles and Basic Ratios

In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse. For a given acute angle θ, the side opposite θ is the opposite side, and the other side (not hypotenuse) is the adjacent side. This lesson teaches how to label the sides and sets the stage for defining the trigonometric ratios.

lessons.title: SOH CAH TOA: Sine, Cosine and Tangent
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches the three primary ratios: sin θ = O/H, cos θ = A/H, tan θ = O/A.

blocks.text: 7.2 SOH CAH TOA: Sine, Cosine and Tangent

SOH CAH TOA is a mnemonic: Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent. This lesson covers using these ratios to find missing sides or angles in right-angled triangles. It includes examples with diagrams and emphasizes the correct identification of sides. These ratios are foundational for all trigonometry.

lessons.title: Special Angles: 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°
lessons.summary: This lesson covers exact values for special angles, derived from equilateral and isosceles right triangles.

blocks.text: Exact values for special angles: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 45° = cos 45° = √2/2, tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3; sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0, tan 90° undefined. This lesson derives these values using equilateral and right-angled triangles, and provides a table for quick reference.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Identities
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces fundamental identities: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ and sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

blocks.text: 7.4 Trigonometric Identities

Two fundamental identities are: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ (from the definition of tangent), and sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 (Pythagorean identity). This lesson teaches how to use these identities to simplify expressions and prove other identities. These identities are essential for solving trigonometric equations and are often tested in JAMB.

lessons.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
lessons.summary: This lesson defines and applies angles of elevation (looking up) and depression (looking down).

blocks.text: 7.5 Angles of Elevation and Depression

Angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when looking up at an object. Angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when looking down. This lesson teaches how to draw and solve problems involving these angles, such as finding the height of a building or the distance to an object.

lessons.title: Bearings and Trigonometry
lessons.summary: This lesson combines bearings with trigonometric ratios for navigation problems.

blocks.text: 7.6 Bearings and Trigonometry

This lesson solves problems involving bearings and distances, using sine, cosine, and tangent to find unknown distances or angles in navigation and surveying. It includes drawing bearing diagrams, using the sine and cosine rules where applicable, and interpreting results in context. Bearings with trigonometry are common in JAMB.

lessons.title: The Sine Rule
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the sine rule for solving non-right-angled triangles.

blocks.text: 7.7 The Sine Rule

The sine rule states: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, where a, b, c are sides opposite angles A, B, C. This lesson covers using the rule to find unknown sides or angles in any triangle, including the ambiguous case (SSA). The sine rule is essential for solving triangles that are not right-angled, and is a key JAMB topic.

lessons.title: The Cosine Rule
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches the cosine rule: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A.

blocks.text: 7.8 The Cosine Rule

The cosine rule relates the sides and angles of any triangle: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A. It is used when two sides and the included angle are known (to find the third side) or when all three sides are known (to find an angle). This lesson provides derivations and examples, and contrasts with the sine rule.

lessons.title: Area of Triangle Using Trigonometry
lessons.summary: This lesson covers the area formula: Area = ½ ab sin C.

blocks.text: 7.9 Area of Triangle Using Trigonometry

The area of a triangle can be computed using two sides and the included angle: Area = ½ a b sin C. This formula is useful when the height is not known. This lesson covers its derivation from the basic area formula, and provides examples with different triangle types. This is a convenient and often tested formula.

lessons.title: Trigonometry: Word Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson solves a variety of word problems using trigonometry, including heights, distances, bearings, and triangle solving.

blocks.text: 7.10 Trigonometry: Word Problems

This lesson applies trigonometry to real-life situations: finding heights of buildings, distances across rivers, bearings, and using sine/cosine rules in practical contexts. Emphasis is on drawing accurate diagrams, identifying the correct trigonometric rule, and solving step by step. These problems are common in JAMB and require careful interpretation.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Equations
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches solving simple trigonometric equations, including using identities.

blocks.text: 7.11 Trigonometric Equations

This lesson covers solving equations like sin θ = k, cos θ = k, tan θ = k, and more complex equations using identities. It includes finding solutions in given intervals (e.g., 0° to 360°). Techniques include using reference angles and the CAST diagram. Trigonometric equations are a JAMB topic that requires careful handling of multiple solutions.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Graphs
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces graphs of sin θ, cos θ, and tan θ, including amplitude, period, and key points.

blocks.text: 7.12 Trigonometric Graphs

Graphs of y = sin θ, y = cos θ, and y = tan θ are periodic. This lesson covers amplitude (for sin/cos), period (360° for sin/cos, 180° for tan), and key points (intercepts, maxima, minima, asymptotes). It also includes simple transformations (amplitude changes, translations). These graphs help in understanding wave motion and solving equations.

lessons.title: Limits: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the concept of limits and evaluating simple limits.

blocks.text: 8.1 Limits: Introduction

A limit describes the value that a function approaches as the input approaches a given point. Notation: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L. This lesson covers intuitive understanding, one-sided limits, and evaluating limits of polynomials and rational functions by substitution and factorization. Limits form the foundation of calculus.

lessons.title: Differentiation: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson defines the derivative as the rate of change or gradient of a curve.

blocks.text: 8.2 Differentiation: Introduction

Differentiation is the process of finding the derivative, which measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function. It is also the gradient of the tangent to a curve. This lesson introduces the concept with examples of average rate vs. instantaneous rate, and the limit definition of derivative: f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h.

lessons.title: Differentiation: The Power Rule
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches the power rule: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹.

blocks.text: 8.3 Differentiation: The Power Rule

The power rule states: if f(x) = xⁿ, then f'(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹. This lesson covers differentiation of terms with positive, negative, and fractional exponents. It also includes the sum, difference, and constant multiple rules. The power rule is the most frequently used differentiation rule in JAMB.

lessons.title: Differentiation of Sums, Differences and Constants
lessons.summary: This lesson extends differentiation to sums, differences, and constant multiples.

blocks.text: 8.4 Differentiation of Sums, Differences and Constants

The derivative of a constant is zero. The derivative of a sum (or difference) is the sum (or difference) of the derivatives. This lesson combines these rules with the power rule to differentiate polynomial functions. It also covers the derivative of a constant times a function: d/dx [c f(x)] = c f'(x).

lessons.title: Gradient of a Curve at a Point
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches finding gradient at a given point by substituting x into the derivative.

blocks.text: 8.5 Gradient of a Curve at a Point
