The derivative f'(x) gives the gradient of the curve y = f(x) at any point x. To find the gradient at a specific point x = a, compute f'(a). This lesson includes examples with polynomials and other functions. The gradient is used to find equations of tangents and normals.

lessons.title: Stationary Points: Maximum and Minimum
lessons.summary: This lesson finds stationary points (where f'(x)=0) and identifies maxima/minima.

blocks.text: 8.6 Stationary Points: Maximum and Minimum

Stationary points occur where the derivative is zero (f'(x)=0). They can be local maxima, minima, or points of inflection. This lesson uses the second derivative test: if f''(x)>0, it's a minimum; if f''(x)<0, it's a maximum; if f''(x)=0, test is inconclusive. The sign chart method is also covered. Stationary points are important in optimization.

lessons.title: Applications of Differentiation
lessons.summary: This lesson applies differentiation to optimization problems and curve sketching.

blocks.text: 8.7 Applications of Differentiation

Differentiation is used to solve optimization problems: finding maximum area, minimum cost, etc. It also helps in sketching curves by analyzing stationary points, intervals of increase/decrease, and concavity. This lesson covers step-by-step problem-solving: define variables, write a function, differentiate, set to zero, and verify. These are common JAMB application questions.

lessons.title: Rates of Change
lessons.summary: This lesson covers rates of change using derivatives, including velocity and acceleration.

blocks.text: 8.8 Rates of Change

Derivatives measure rates of change. In kinematics, velocity is the rate of change of displacement (v = ds/dt), and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (a = dv/dt). This lesson also covers other rates like population growth, cooling, and flow rates. Problems involve finding rates at specific times.

lessons.title: Integration: Introduction
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces integration as the reverse of differentiation, with the constant of integration.

blocks.text: 8.9 Integration: Introduction

Integration is the inverse process of differentiation. The indefinite integral of a function f(x) is a function F(x) such that F'(x) = f(x). This is written as ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration. This lesson covers basic integration rules and the concept of antiderivatives.

lessons.title: Integration: The Power Rule
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches the power rule for integration: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C (n≠-1).

blocks.text: 8.10 Integration: The Power Rule

The power rule for integration is: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C, for n ≠ -1. This lesson covers integrating polynomial functions and functions with negative and fractional exponents. The special case n = -1 is the natural logarithm: ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C. This rule is the foundation of indefinite integration.

lessons.title: Definite Integrals and Area Under Curves
lessons.summary: This lesson covers definite integrals and using them to find area under curves.

blocks.text: 8.11 Definite Integrals and Area Under Curves

A definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx gives the signed area between the curve y=f(x) and the x-axis from x=a to x=b. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), where F is an antiderivative. This lesson covers evaluating definite integrals and finding areas between curves.

lessons.title: Calculus: Word Problems
lessons.summary: This lesson applies differentiation and integration to word problems involving rates, optimization, and area.

blocks.text: 8.12 Calculus: Word Problems

This lesson solves practical problems: maximum profit, minimum surface area, velocity and distance from acceleration, area between curves, etc. Emphasis is on setting up the mathematical model (function or equation), applying differentiation or integration, and interpreting the results. These problems are common in JAMB and require a clear understanding of calculus concepts.

lessons.title: Data Types and Collection
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces data types (qualitative/quantitative, discrete/continuous) and methods of collection.

blocks.text: 9.1 Data Types and Collection

Data is information collected for analysis. Qualitative data is categorical (e.g., gender, colour); quantitative data is numerical. Quantitative data can be discrete (countable, e.g., number of children) or continuous (measurable, e.g., height). Data collection methods include surveys, experiments, and observations. This lesson provides a foundation for statistical analysis.

lessons.title: Frequency Tables
lessons.summary: This lesson covers constructing frequency tables for ungrouped and grouped data.

blocks.text: 9.2 Frequency Tables

A frequency table organizes data by showing the frequency (count) of each value or class interval. For grouped data, class intervals, class boundaries, and class midpoints are used. This lesson teaches how to construct frequency tables, calculate cumulative frequencies, and interpret the information.

lessons.title: Mean of Ungrouped Data
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches calculating the mean (average) of ungrouped data.

blocks.text: 9.3 Mean of Ungrouped Data

The mean (or average) of ungrouped data is the sum of all data values divided by the number of values: x̄ = Σx / n. This lesson covers calculation, interpretation, and properties of the mean, including the effect of outliers. The mean is the most common measure of central tendency.

lessons.title: Median and Mode of Ungrouped Data
lessons.summary: This lesson covers finding median (middle value) and mode (most frequent) for ungrouped data.

blocks.text: 9.4 Median and Mode of Ungrouped Data

The median is the middle value when data is arranged in order. If n is odd, median is the (n+1)/2 th value; if even, it is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the value that appears most frequently. This lesson covers finding both, and when each is appropriate (e.g., median for skewed data).

lessons.title: Mean of Grouped Data
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches calculating the mean of grouped data using class midpoints.

blocks.text: 9.5 Mean of Grouped Data

For grouped data, the mean is estimated by: x̄ = Σ(f × x) / Σf, where x is the class midpoint and f is the frequency. This lesson teaches how to construct the table, calculate midpoints, and compute the mean. The result is an approximation of the true mean.

lessons.title: Median and Mode of Grouped Data
lessons.summary: This lesson covers finding median and mode for grouped data using interpolation.

blocks.text: 9.6 Median and Mode of Grouped Data

The median for grouped data is found using the cumulative frequency and the formula: Median = L + [ (N/2 - CF) / f ] × w, where L is lower boundary of median class, CF is cumulative frequency before median class, f is frequency of median class, w is class width. The mode is estimated from the modal class (highest frequency). This lesson provides step-by-step methods.

lessons.title: Measures of Dispersion: Range
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces range (max-min) as a measure of spread.

blocks.text: 9.7 Measures of Dispersion: Range

The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values in a data set. It is the simplest measure of dispersion but is sensitive to outliers. This lesson covers calculation, interpretation, and when it is useful. It also introduces the concept of dispersion as a complement to central tendency.

lessons.title: Variance and Standard Deviation
lessons.summary: This lesson covers variance and standard deviation for both ungrouped and grouped data.

blocks.text: 9.8 Variance and Standard Deviation

Variance is the average of the squared deviations from the mean: σ² = Σ(x - x̄)² / n (population) or s² = Σ(x - x̄)² / (n-1) (sample). Standard deviation is σ = √σ². For grouped data, use frequencies. This lesson provides formulas, calculations, and interpretation. Standard deviation is the most common measure of spread.

lessons.title: Quartiles and Interquartile Range
lessons.summary: This lesson covers quartiles (Q₁, Q₂, Q₃) and interquartile range (IQR = Q₃ - Q₁).

blocks.text: 9.9 Quartiles and Interquartile Range

Quartiles divide data into four equal parts: Q₁ (25th percentile), Q₂ (median, 50th percentile), Q₃ (75th percentile). The interquartile range (IQR) is Q₃ - Q₁, representing the middle 50% of the data. This lesson covers finding quartiles for both ungrouped and grouped data, and using IQR to detect outliers.

lessons.title: Bar Charts and Pie Charts
lessons.summary: This lesson teaches construction and interpretation of bar charts and pie charts.
